prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical time standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I have tested the case against what I normally ask of a claimed advance: has it been confirmed independently, was the credited contribution decisive, and will it last. Magic-wavelength trapping is one clear idea that removed the light-shift limit on a narrow optical transition and let thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. Strontium, ytterbium and mercury lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level have since been built and compared by groups on several continents, with agreeing frequency ratios. That is the calibration and systematics record I trust. The clocks resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and constrain varying constants and dark-matter couplings, so the physics will last whatever the metrology bodies decide about the second. Five of eight members converged on the same two names, and I do not count that as a substitute for the science, but the science and the attribution both hold up when I look at them independently. I have not moved to a two-part configuration. Any second part would have to be a single person from a part with three or four names, and I see no candidate that fits honestly.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and I accept that the committee could read lattice clocks as the best-engineered successor in a line already honoured. I also cannot settle from my own expertise the priority between Katori and the JILA group, or the weight of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg and Hinkley, and the citation will fail if an expert reviewer finds Ye's role was accuracy work built on Katori's concept rather than a co-invention. The pending redefinition of the second is a confirming milestone, not a condition. Finally, a clock is less obviously a discovery about nature than IceCube is, and I disclose that this is where my own taste pulls the other way.

responses.point: Danielsson holds IceCube (B010) as a discovery in the plainest sense, with Halzen and Karle, confirmed through several channels, and argues that waiting does not make it firmer.
responses.response: I agree the diffuse flux is established and I started the opening with IceCube first. I still do not move it to the top, for two reasons you also give. First, the credit: Halzen and Karle leave out Yoshida and the AMANDA lineage, and I cannot defend a two-name cut in a collaboration of hundreds without an expert history of who did what in the diffuse-flux analysis. Second, the sources are at a few sigma, and neither KM3NeT nor Baikal-GVD yet gives a comparable second telescope. I would call this a year to wait, not a rejection. If the experts report that Halzen and Karle are clearly the decisive pair, B010 is my first alternative, and I would ask you what evidence on the roles would make you accept a three-name set.

responses.point: Eriksson holds magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B029) as a prediction followed by confirmation, with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero, and says clocks are the fallback if recognition is judged premature.
responses.response: Your answer to my round-1 question was honest, and I now read your ranking of clocks as deference to atomic colleagues, not a physical objection, which I accept. On B029, the prediction-then-confirmation structure is persuasive, but the experimental first author Yuan Cao is outside the three names, the pairing mechanism is open, and the sample-quality history is recent. As an experimentalist I want a few more years of independent reproduction before fixing the credit. Nothing in that argument is a reason to leave out clocks, which are the most mature candidate. I keep B029 as an alternative and would reconsider if the expert reports say the credit can be drawn cleanly.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B043 with the wording 'invention and realisation', warns about the lineage of 2005 and 2012, and notes that Ye's scope across combs, clocks and molecules makes the citation delicate.
responses.response: I agree with your wording and have kept 'invention and realisation' in the citation, together with the magic-wavelength mechanism so that it is clearly separate from the comb and ion-trapping prizes. A comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and a trapped ion is one quantum system. The lattice clock is a different thing, a many-atom clock with a cancelled light shift, and that is why it overtook the others in stability. I would not credit Ye for combs or molecules. Since you know the community better than I do, can you say whether the lattice-clock story is told differently in Europe, where Lemonde and Katori are both given as the origin of the idea?

responses.point: Kroll supports B043 for the development of lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level and says the main impact so far is inside metrology and fundamental-physics tests, with the redefinition of the second not yet done.
responses.response: I take your practical point that the impact is still mostly within metrology, and I would not claim otherwise in the citation. I prefer 'invention and realisation' to 'development', because 'development' can be read to cover every group that improved the clock and so dilutes the credit to two. I also think we should not make the redefinition a test for the prize. It is a decision for a metrology body and will probably follow the science, so waiting for it would just let others set our timetable.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase (B020) for Halperin, Nelson and Young as a simple universal mechanism, and accepts the weak opening support and the overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: The Halperin-Nelson-Young mechanism is elegant and I respect the argument that the authors should be honoured while they can be. I am a detector builder, so I weigh the experimental history, and you note it yourself: the hexatic phase was firmly established only in particular colloidal and film systems and the first-order versus continuous question is system-dependent. Together with the 2016 overlap that leaves me unable to put B020 in my configuration. I will not leave your case unanswered: I would ask what the strongest experimental confirmation of the hexatic phase is, and whether you would join B043 if the condensed-matter experts found the same system dependence.

uncertainties: Priority and decisive credit between Katori's group and Ye's group, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto or others should enter the names. This needs an expert reviewer on the early history, and it could change my position.
Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, which the citation wording is meant to help with but cannot guarantee.
The IceCube credit (Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, AMANDA) is unresolved, so I cannot judge whether waiting a year changes the answer for B010.
Whether magic-angle graphene needs more consolidation, in particular on the pairing mechanism and the credit for Yuan Cao.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I am an astroparticle experimentalist in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which may bias me toward IceCube (B010), and I continue to disclose that; I have no apparent connection to the IceCube or lattice-clock groups. As Chair I will keep running the process neutrally and I do not treat support counts as a substitute for the scientific case.
